For example, the matrix

$$B = [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$$

is nilpotent because its second power is the zero matrix:

$$\begin{aligned}{B}^{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ & =O\end{aligned}$$

To state the definition more precisely: a matrix with the property $B^k=O$ for a number $k>0$ is known as a **nilpotent** matrix, and the lowest number $k$ such that $B^k=O$ is called the **index.**

Therefore, our matrix $B$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "39a61f3b-3f47-5962-a20c-33867d6f1127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3130 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fbfd42f1-c449-5a1c-89f3-22f0da76f2bc" :step/math-academy-id 17047 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184918}} {:db/id 17592186184921 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185316 :tutorial/content "A matrix is said to be **idempotent**, when multiplied by itself, yields itself.
